Biochemical methane potential from sewage sludge: Effect of an aerobic
pretreatment and ﬂy ash addition as source of trace elements
César Huiliñir a,⇑, Paula Pinto-Villegas a, Alejandra Castillo a, Silvio Montalvo a, Lorna Guerrero b
a Departamento de Ingeniería Química, Universidad de Santiago de Chile, Santiago, Chile
b Departamento de Ingeniería Química y Ambiental, Universidad Técnica Federico Santa Marıa, Valparaıso, Chile
a r t i c l e
i n f o
Article history:
Received 12 October 2016
Revised 8 February 2017
Accepted 13 March 2017
Available online 18 March 2017
Keywords:
Aerobic pretreatment
Fly ash
Combined effect
Methane generation
Mixed sludge
a b s t r a c t
The effect of aerobic pretreatment and ﬂy ash addition on the production of methane from mixed sludge
is studied. Three assays with pretreated and not pretreated mixed sludge in the presence of ﬂy ash (con-
centrations of 0, 10, 25, 50, 250 and 500 mg/L) were run at mesophilic condition. It was found that the
combined use of aerobic pretreatment and ﬂy ash addition increases methane production up to 70% when
the ﬂy ash concentrations were lower than 50 mg/L, while concentrations higher than 250 mg/L cause up
to 11% decrease of methane production. For the anaerobic treatment of mixed sludge without pretreat-
ment, the ﬂy ash improved methane generation at all the concentrations studied, with a maximum of
56%. The removal of volatile solids does not show an improvement compared to the separate use of an
aerobic pre-treatment and ﬂy ash addition. Therefore, the combined use of the aerobic pre-treatment
and ﬂy ash addition improves only the production of methane.

1. Introduction
Nowadays the continuous production of large amounts of sew-
age sludge is becoming a worldwide environmental problem (Zhao
et al., 2010). Thus, emphasis in sludge management has shifted
from its disposal to the beneﬁcial use of itself and its products.
Among sludge treatment technologies, anaerobic digestion (AD)
is a well-established and proven method. It transforms organic
matter into biogas (60–70 vol% of methane, CH4), destroys most
of the pathogens present in the sludge, limits possible odor prob-
lems associated with residual putrescible matter, and reduces the
amount of ﬁnal sludge solids for disposal (Appels et al., 2008).
However, the application of AD to sewage sludge is often limited
by very long retention times (20–30 days) and a low overall degra-
dation efﬁciency of the organic dry solids (30–50%). These limiting
factors are generally associated with the hydrolysis stage (Tiehm
et al., 2001). In order to improve this step, several sewage sludge
pretreatments have been proposed, which include biological (lar-
gely thermal phase anaerobic), thermal hydrolysis, mechanical
(ultrasound, high pressure, and lysis), chemical with oxidation
and alkali treatments (Ennouri et al., 2016; Neumann et al.,
2016). Among the biological methods, micro-aerobic pretreatment
has been proposed (Girotto et al., 2016; Mata-Alvarez et al., 2000;
Montalvo et al., 2016). It was reported that the limited oxygen sup-
ply caused an increase of the hydrolysis rates in the case of com-
plex organic matter in batch tests (Johansen and Bakke, 2006), an
improvement in digester performance, and a reduction of volatile
fatty acid concentration (Diaz et al., 2011). Furthermore, the
micro-aerobic step can be directly performed in the same unit
prior to anaerobic digestion. This pretreatment has been used suc-
cessfully to treat sewage sludge at the laboratory scale (Montalvo
et al., 2016), increasing methane generation as well as volatile
solids degradation.
In addition to pretreatment challenges, existing trace elements
are insufﬁcient for anaerobic microorganisms when solid waste,
such as organic fractions of municipal solid waste or sewage
sludge, is used alone as a feedstock for anaerobic digestion
(Moestedt et al., 2016). The literature has emphasized the impor-
tance of supplementing trace elements for maximum methano-
genic activity (Choong et al., 2016; Romero-Guiza et al., 2016;
Thanh et al., 2016). Although the importance of this parameter is
clear, its control is limited mainly by the high cost of the trace salts
used for this purpose. In this context, the use of a cheaper source of
trace elements could help control this parameter without addi-
tional expenses (Huilinir et al., 2015). A source of trace metals is
ﬂy ash (FA), which has been applied to the anaerobic digestion of
municipal solid waste (Lo et al., 2010; Romero-Guiza et al., 2016)
and recently to sewage sludge coming from the pulp and paper
industry (Huilinir et al., 2015). The inclusion of ﬂy ash in both cases

increases methane production and also reduces the concentration
of volatile solids (VS). However, the use of ﬂy ash in the anaerobic
digestion of sewage sludge has not been presented yet. Therefore,
an analysis of the effect of ﬂy ash on the anaerobic digestion of
sewage sludge in the presence of trace elements is necessary.
Even though the use of a pretreatment and the use of ﬂy ash as
trace elements source had shown positive effects separately, the
use of a combination both in the same substrate has not been stud-
ied yet. Only Mansour et al. (2012) compared the effect of an aer-
obic pretreatment and addition of bottom ashes (as pre-treatment)
separately on anaerobic digestion of municipal solid waste, focus-
ing on the kinetic of the process, without using the aerobic
pretreatment and the bottom ashes combined. On the other hand,
Liu et al. (2015) studying the anaerobic digestion of corn stover
indicated that NaOH pretreatment and the addition of trace ele-
ments (Fe, Co and Ni) improve the biodegradability of corn stover
and enhance biomethane production, and the present study is the
only one that has dealt with the combined effect of pretreatment
and trace element supplementation. Thus, the aim of the present
work was to determine the combined effect of an aerobic pretreat-
ment and the addition of ﬂy ash as trace element source on
methane production and VS reduction in a batch system. To the
best of our knowledge, the combined effect of an aerobic pretreat-
ment and ﬂy ash as trace element source have not been reported
previously. The effect of ﬂy ash as the sole source of trace elements
was also determined.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Experimental setup
A 1-L glass reactor operating with an effective volume of
900 mL
was
used
for
the
aerobic
pretreatment.
In
each
pretreatment air was injected continuously into the bioreactors
by mini-compressors (0–10 l per minute, lpm) and distributed by
small diffusers. The air ﬂow rate (AFR) was calibrated before the
pretreatment assays using the volume variation method. The con-
ditions used for pretreatment were 0.35 vvm (air volume per liquid
volume per minute) for 48 h at 35 C, according to Montalvo et al.
(2016). After aerobic pretreatment, pretreated sludge was fed to
several batch anaerobic digesters of 280 mL of total volume.
For the anaerobic process, every experimental run considered
the installation of twelve 280-mL anaerobic mini-digesters with
effective operating volumes of 250 mL each. Eight of them were
meant for measuring parameters in the liquid phase (chemical
oxygen demand (COD) and volatile solids, and four were used to
measure methane by liquid displacement according to Huilinir
et al. (2015). The mini-digesters operated in discontinuous mode
for 43 days, at which time the system reached a steady state. The
digesters were stirred manually once or twice per day before read-
ing the volume displaced by methane.
The volume of the digesters was completed with distilled water,
they were stoppered with rubber stoppers and sealed with white
silicone to ensure anaerobiosis, and they were covered with
aluminum foil to prevent the growth of photosynthetic organisms.
All the runs were carried out in duplicate.
2.2. Inocula, substrate and experimental design
The inoculum was obtained from an anaerobic reactor of the La
Farfana Water Treatment Plant of Aguas Andinas in Santiago, Chile.
The inoculum had 0.59 ± 0.01 g VS/g of total solids (TS), 2.2 ± 0.42 g
of soluble COD/L, and a pH of 7.23 ± 0.12. The substrate was mixed
sludge (a mixture of primary (60%) and secondary (40%) sludge)
also from the La Farfana Water Treatment Plant. The substrate pre-
sented a ratio of 0.76 ± 0.01 g VS/g TS, 5.87 ± 0.87 g/L of soluble
COD, and a pH of 5.69 ± 0.32. The main trace elements found in
the
mixed
sludge
were:
Cd
(1.2 mg/kg),
Zn
(3.19 mg/kg),
Fe (1.80 mg/kg), Al (1.58 mg/kg), Zn (3.19 mg/kg), Cr (1.80 mg/kg),
Cu (2.06 mg/kg), Ni (2.24 mg/kg), Mn (2.51 mg/kg), Ba (2.09 mg/kg),
Co (0.8 mg/kg), B (0.74 mg/kg), Pb (2.09 mg/kg) and Se (2.77 mg/kg).
The sewage sludge was refrigerated at 4 C for no more than
3 days until its use.
The ﬂy ash was obtained from a thermoelectric power plant,
with a particle diameter between 0.12 and 0.2 mm. The ash was
taken from electrostatic precipitators used to collect particulate
matter generated by the combustion of bituminous coal, placed
before the gaseous efﬂuents leave the plant. The main trace ele-
ments found in them were Fe (4.24 g/kg), Al (1.37 g/kg), Zn
(5.8 mg/kg), Cr (3.93 mg/kg), Cu (2.32 mg/kg), Ni (3.85 mg/kg),
Mn (37.7 mg/kg), V (26.4 mg/kg), Ba (64 mg/kg), Co (0.9 mg/kg),
and B (25.4 mg/kg). Since the ﬂy ash used in all the experiments
came from the same sample obtained in situ from the thermoelec-
tric power plant, the mass of trace elements used in all the exper-
iments was proportional to the mass reported here.
In each anaerobic treatment, the substrate/inoculum ratio (F/I)
was 1.5 g VS substrate/g VS inoculum according to Tomei et al.
(2008). For each assay two weekly measurements of soluble and
total COD and suspended VS were made in duplicate. The temper-
ature in the container was kept at 35 C using three automatically
controlled aquarium heaters. Three assays were made in order to
see the effect of ﬂy ash and aerobic pretreatment, both separately
and combined, as shown in Table 1. The ﬁrst and second assays
were ran on pretreated sludge (P) and different ﬂy ash (FA) concen-
trations. The third assay was only meant to see the effect of ﬂy ash
on the anaerobic digestion.
2.3. Chemical analyses
The following parameters were determined: soluble COD and
VS. COD was measured by a colorimetric method according to
APHA (2012) and volatile solids (VS) were also measured according
to APHA (2012).
Methane production was measured by volumetric displace-
ment, connecting inverted Falcon tubes containing 3% w/w NaOH
solution to remove CO2 and H2S as main impurities from the bio-
gas, displacing only the methane volume. The resulting biogas
travels through the ﬂexible tubing to the Falcon tube, where it
comes in contact with the NaOH solution, forming Na2CO3 and
Na2S and bubbling only methane. The methane collected in the

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Effect on methane production
Fig. 1 shows the methane accumulated for the three assays. In
Fig. 1 and Table 2 it is seen that pretreatment improved methane
production compared with the system without pretreatment and
without FA. For the ﬁrst assay (Fig. 1a) the aerobic pretreatment
increased methane production from 263 to 340 mL/ginitial
VS
(29%); the second assay (Fig. 1b) showed a 30% increase (from
171 to 221 mL/ginitial VS), and in assay three (Fig. 1c) there is also
an increase of up to 47% (from 195 to 287 mL/ginitialVS). This last
value (47%) was higher than those obtained in assays 2 and 3,
and it can be attributed to the different effect of the pre-
treatment on the composition and biodegradability of the sub-
strate used in each anaerobic assay. The pre-aeration process, used
here as an extra step where the sludge was aerated uninterrupt-
edly during 48 h, improved the solubility of organic matter, making
the rapidly biodegradable organic matter available to the fermen-
tative and methanogenic biomass (Montalvo et al., 2016). The
increase of the methanogenic activity can also be attributed to an
improvement in the growth of facultative anaerobic microorgan-
isms, which can keep a low redox potential, providing the best con-
ditions for the growth of strict anaerobes (Mshandete et al., 2005).
It is important to mention that the oxygen concentrations mea-
sured in the pre-aeration step were nil (not detected by sensors)
under the aeration condition. Thus, the condition of ‘‘micro-
aeration”, i.e., oxygen concentration lower than 1 L O2/L feed
(Krayzelova et al., 2015) was accomplished and also showed that
oxygen does not affect the anaerobic process after an aerobic
pre-treatment (Montalvo et al., 2016).
The improvement in the methane generation agrees with the
results presented by Montalvo et al. (2016), who reported an
increase of up to 200% in accumulated methane when the sewage
sludge was pretreated aerobically. Fu et al. (2015) also reported
better performance of anaerobic digestion when the substrate
(corn straw) was subjected to microaerobic pretreatment, increas-
ing biogas production. Mansour et al. (2012) using pre-aeration for
fresh municipal solid waste, found a signiﬁcant advantage of the
aerobic pretreatment over the control, with a much better perfor-
mance of methanogenesis (higher methane production). The same
trend was reported by Xu et al. (2014), who found an increase
(between 5% and 18%) in methane generation in reactors with food
waste pretreated aerobically. Thus, it is shown that pre-aeration
can be used as pretreatment to increase methane yield in a batch
system also for sewage sludge.
Fig. 1 also shows the effect of ﬂy ash on the process. According
to the results, the ﬂy ash has different effects on methane produc-
tion depending on whether the sewage sludge was subjected to
pretreatment or not. When the sewage sludge was not pretreated
(Fig. 1c), the effect of ﬂy ash was always positive, with an increase
in methane production varying from 15% at a ﬂy ash concentration
of 500 mg/L to 56% at a ﬂy ash concentration of 50 mg/L, with the
best performance between 10 and 50 mg/L (Table 2). In the range
of 10–250 mg/L of ﬂy ash, the accumulated methane does not show
statistically signiﬁcant differences (p > 0.05). A different situation
was found for sewage sludge pretreated aerobically. Fig. 1a and
Table 2 show decreasing methane production with respect to the
NP-NFA1 assay at high ﬂy ash concentrations, and decreasing
methane production of 4% and 11% at ﬂy ash concentrations of
250 and 500 mg/L, respectively. At lower ﬂy ash concentrations
(Fig. 1b) there is between 30 and 70% increase in methane produc-
tion compared to the raw process (NP-NFA2), with the highest
methane production achieved at 25 mg/L of FA (Table 2). It must
be mentioned that statistically signiﬁcant differences were deter-
mined in all the experiments with pretreatment compared to the
assay of the pretreated sludge but without ﬂy ash.
In order to see the effect of the ﬂy ash on the assays separated
from the effect of pretreatment (assays 2 and 3), methane produc-
tion in the presence of FA was compared with the experiment
without FA but with pretreatment (P-NFA); for the process without
pretreatment the comparison was made with respect to the system
without pretreatment and without ﬂy ash (NP-NFA). The results
are shown in Fig. 2, where it is seen that the FA in the aerobically
pretreated system causes a strong inhibition of methane produc-
tion, decreasing the methane accumulated when the ﬂy ash con-
centrations are higher than 50 mg/L, with the highest decreasing
around 30%. On the contrary, for the process without pretreatment,
the effects of all the ﬂy ash concentrations were positive, showing
in
all
cases
statistically
signiﬁcant
differences
(p < 0.05)
in
methane production with respect to the NP-NFA assay.
The positive effect of FA on the process obtained in this study
agrees with other studies and can be related to the trace element
concentrations in the FA. It is known that trace elements are nec-
essary for a good anaerobic digestion performance. Zhang et al.
(2011) indicated that the supplementation of trace elements in
wastewater improved the performance of anaerobic digestion in
terms of methane generation and volatile fatty acids decrease.
Zhang and Jahng (2012) indicated that supplementation with trace
elements keeps methane generation and pH constant in a continu-
ous operation, showing that Fe was identiﬁed as the element that
mostly affects this behavior. A similar situation was indicated by
Facchin et al. (2013), who found that the mesophilic anaerobic
digestion of food waste with two different inoculums improved
methane production when the waste was supplemented with Se.
The mechanism for accelerating and improving methane genera-
tion may be associated with the effect of trace elements on differ-
ent types of enzymes, especially the metalloenzymes. According to
the literature (Choong et al., 2016), the trace elements in the met-
alloenzyme are functioning to form the active site, the cofactor,
and the structure itself. The general trace element requirement
trend for metalloenzymes in methanogenesis can be simpliﬁed as

Fe  Ni > Co > Zn = Mo/W (Choong et al., 2016; Glass and Orphan,
2012). This order is predicted without considering the substrate
medium, which will shift the enzyme ratios, and hence alter the
corresponding trace element requirement (Choong et al., 2016).
On the other hand, the negative effect seen with certain concen-
trations in this work has also been reported in the literature. Park
et al. (2010), using simulated wastewater as substrate at 35 C,
showed that acetoclastic methanogens were not stimulated by
nutrient supplementation at relatively low concentrations and a
slight perturbation was observed when supplementation was at a
relatively high concentration. Yue et al. (2007) studied the
anaerobic digestion of cattail by rumen cultures in the presence
of Cu(II), Cd(II) and Cr(VI), showing that low heavy metal
concentrations
(Cu(II)
2.4 mg/L,
Cd(II)
1.6 mg/L
and
Cr(VI)
4.0 mg/L) promoted cattail degradation and methane production,
but there is a severe inhibition of the cattail degradation at high
heavy metal dosage. The chemical binding of heavy metals to the
enzymes and subsequent disruption of the enzyme structure and
function are the main causes of this toxic effect (Appels et al.,
2008).
In order to explain the effect of ﬂy ash on the process, it is nec-
essary to see the different kinds of metals presents in the ﬂy ash
and how they may affect the process. Table 3 shows the elements
and their effects reported in the literature, while Table 4 shows the
concentration determined in each ﬂy ash concentration used.
According to this information, it can be said that Mn and Fe are
the only trace elements whose concentrations are in the range
found in the literature and reported as stimulatory and only when
the ﬂy ash concentrations are very high. Therefore, it is not possi-
ble to indicate which trace elements are affecting the process pos-
itively or negatively. However, because trace elements (mainly
heavy metals) are present as mixtures, possible speciﬁc antagonis-
tic and synergistic effects can explain the ﬂy ash effect (Chen et al.,
2014). Synergism means the enhanced toxic effect of one metal in
the presence of small amounts of another metal, while antagonism
refers to the effect of one metal which alleviates the toxic effect of
another metal (Chen et al., 2014). For example, Oleszkiewicz and
Sharma (1988) showed that aluminum silicate is an antagonist of
the toxicity of other heavy metals. Earlier, Babich and Stotzky
(1983) showed that nickel was synergistic in Ni–Cu, Ni–Mo–Co,
and Ni–Hg systems, and antagonistic in Ni–Zn and Ni–Cd systems
(Chen et al., 2014). Thus, it is the mixture of trace elements present
in the FA and their interaction, and not the effect of only one trace
element, that can explain the effect of ﬂy ash in this study.
According to the results obtained in the assays, the combination
of an aerobic pretreatment and ﬂy ash supplementation improved
methane generation in comparison with a process only pretreated
or only supplemented with ﬂy ash, at least in a certain range of ﬂy
ash concentrations. This situation can be seen clearly in Fig. 2 and
Table 2, where the combination of pretreatment and the use of
25 mg/L of ﬂy ash increased methane production by up to 70%,
while the use of pretreatment alone could increase methane gener-
ation by 48% and the use of only ﬂy ash (assay 3) increased
methane generation by up to 56%. However, the combination also
decreases methane production when the ﬂy ash concentrations are
greater than 100 mg/L, as shown in Fig. 2. From these two effect it
is possible to infer that: (i) Anaerobic digestion with pretreated
sewage sludge required lower doses of trace elements, which
was necessary only for the biological steps (acidogenesis, acetoge-
nesis, and methanogenesis), and (ii) in raw sludge (without pre-
treatment), ﬂy ash can inﬂuence both the biological steps and
the hydrolytic step. This point can be seen in the greater VS
removal obtained for the experiments without aerobic pretreat-
ment, where the VS removal in the presence of ﬂy ash was always
greater than that of the system without ﬂy ash, with the exception
of the system with a ﬂy ash concentration of 25 mg/L. The effect of

also indicated that the use of FeO on the acidogenic reactor of

the sewage sludge was pretreated could be explained as an excess
of trace elements that was not used in the hydrolytic step.
According to these results, the combination of an aerobic pre-
treatment and ﬂy ash as a source of trace elements improved
methane production compared to the effect of ﬂy ash and pretreat-
ment separately, when ﬂy ash concentrations are lower than
50 mg/L. Without pretreatment, the ﬂy ash improved methane
generation at all the concentrations studied (10–500 mg/L), with
the best results in the range of 10–50 mg/L.
3.2. Effect of ﬂy ash and aerobic pretreatment on volatile solids and
soluble COD removal
Fig. 3 shows the concentrations of volatile solids (VS) and sol-
uble COD in all the assays, while Fig. 4 shows the different removal
percentages obtained. For the VS (Fig. 3a and b), it is seen that VS
concentration decreases in both cases (with and without pretreat-
ment), with the greatest decrease occurring during the ﬁrst
15 days. This behavior indicates that the hydrolytic and acidogenic
steps are predominant in the ﬁrst days. According to the statistical
analysis, there were no signiﬁcant differences (p > 0.05) in VS con-
centrations between processes at different ﬂy ash concentrations
(Fig. 3a and b). Nevertheless, the trends of Fig. 3a and b showed
that the process had a higher hydrolysis rate in the system without
aerobic pretreatment in the ﬁrst 15 days (Fig. 3b). Indeed, the aver-
age hydrolysis rate in the system with pretreatment in the ﬁrst
15 days (determined on the slope observed on linear regression)
was 423.89 ± 77.55 mg VS/L d, 15% lower than the average
hydrolysis rate observed in the system without pre-treatment
(501.43 ± 56.26 mg VS/L d). This situation indicates that the aero-
bic pretreatment degraded a part of the VS, decreasing the hydrol-
ysis rate in the anaerobic step.
As shown in Fig. 4a, for the case with pretreatment the highest
VS removal was around 33% and was obtained in the assay without
ﬂy ash (P-NFA), while the lowest VS removal occurred at ﬂy ash
concentrations of 25 and 50 mg/L, with 25% of VS removal. This
behavior can be explained by the less biodegradable (hydrolysable)
VS available in the system with pre-treated mixed sludge, in con-
junction with the more highly soluble COD concentrations avail-
able
for
methanogenesis.
This
availability
allows
the
methanogenic biomass to generate higher methane volumes with-
out the need to hydrolyse more VS, which had been already
degraded (at least a portion) in the aerobic pre-treatment. This sit-
uation can be observed too in the degradation of soluble COD in the
ﬁrst 15 days (Fig. 3c), where the decrease of soluble COD was more
pronounced in the reactors with ﬂy ash addition. Finally, the
greater soluble COD removal obtained in the experiments with
pre-treated sludge and ﬂy ash addition in concentrations lower
than 50 mg/L (Fig. 4b) also indicated that higher methane volumes
are related to higher soluble COD removal. This also agreed with
the higher methane production in the ﬁrst 15 days (See Supple-
mentary data) for the experiments with 10 and 25 mg/L of ﬂy ash.
On the other hand, at higher ﬂy ash concentrations (P-50, P-250
and P-500) there is lower methane production compared to the
process with pretreatment and without ﬂy ash (P-NFA), and there-
fore VS degradation was also slower.
Finally, there were signiﬁcant differences (p < 0.05) in VS
removal between processes with and without pretreatment with
ﬂy ash concentrations of 10, 25 and 50 mg/L.
It is important to note that the pre-treatment has an effect on
the VS content. The original VS content in the mixed sludge was
0.76 ± 0.01 gVS/gTS, while after the pre-treatment it decreased to
0.73 ± 0.01 gVS/gTS, a value that indicated that the pre-treatment
decreases the VS content in the mixed sludge. The decrease of
the VS content in mixed sludge due to aerobic pre-treatment was
analyzed in Montalvo et al. (2016), who indicated that an air ﬂow
rate of 0.3 vvm produced a 36% increase of the VSS hydrolysis rate
compared to the system without pre-treatment. Therefore, the aer-
obic pre-treatment produces a faster hydrolysis rate of VS and also
decreases the VS content available for anaerobic digestion.
The VS removal obtained in the pretreated sewage sludge was
lower than that reported elsewhere. Fu et al. (2016) obtained
50% VS removal for a thermophilic anaerobic digestion of corn
straw, while Montalvo et al. (2016) reported that the removal
was as high as 68%. The differences can be related to the type of
substrate and also the different initial VS concentrations used in
each case.
For the case without pretreatment (Fig. 4a), the tendency of VS
removal was different, because the highest VS removal was
achieved in the presence of ﬂy ash. In this case, the process without
pretreatment and without ﬂy ash (NP-NFA) has a low VS removal
(around 30%), showing that, as mentioned earlier, the addition of
ﬂy ash probably improved the hydrolytic step. The highest VS
removal (around 40%) was obtained with 50 mg/L of ﬂy ash, and
the lowest removal (28%) with 25 mg/L of ﬂy ash, which also
showed one of the highest methane productions (Table 2). These
results agree with the results obtained by Huilinir et al. (2015),
but it results do not agree with those reported by Lo et al.
(2009), who studied the use of ﬂy ash on the anaerobic digestion
of municipal solid waste. They indicated that VS removal was
lower in the system with ﬂy ash because under these conditions
the microbial activity was higher, as reﬂected in higher methane

Regarding soluble COD, different concentration proﬁles were
obtained with and without pretreatment. When the sewage sludge
was pretreated (Fig. 3c), there was a clear decrease in all the assays,
with the initial soluble COD concentration (around 6500 mg COD/
L) higher than that in the anaerobic process without pretreatment,
mainly because the aerobic pretreatment increased the hydrolysis
efﬁciency.
Indeed,
the
concentration
of
soluble
COD
before
the aerobic pre-treatment was 5.87 ± 0.87 g/L, while after the
pre-treatment it increased up to 10.4 ± 0.04 g/L. These high con-
centrations also explain the high removal of soluble COD achieved
in these assays, which was greater than 40% (Fig. 4b). It is impor-
tant to note that the soluble COD consumption rate (determined
from the slopes found for the linear regressions) in the ﬁrst 15 days
of the experiments was higher in the system with ﬂy ash up to
50 mg/L. For instance, the soluble COD consumption rate in the
system without ﬂy ash addition was 223.91 mg COD/L d, while
at concentrations of 10, 25 and 50 mg/L the COD consumption rate
was 362.96, 481.03 and 511.53 mg COD/L d, respectively.
These values also agreed with the higher methane volume pro-
duced in these experiments (see Supplementary data). Therefore,
the ﬂy ash addition up to values of 50 mg/L increased the soluble
COD consumption rate in the process.
The removal percentage of soluble COD (Fig. 4b) is greater at
lower ﬂy ash values compared to the process with pretreatment
and without ﬂy ash, while at high ﬂy ash concentrations (P-250
and P-500) the soluble COD removal was lower than in the process
without ﬂy ash (P-NFA). This behavior is in good agreement with
the tendency observed for methane production (Fig. 2), where it
was seen that high ﬂy ash concentrations decrease methane
production.
When the sewage sludge was not pretreated, the initial soluble
COD concentrations were low (close to 4000 mg/L) compared to
those of the system with pretreatment, and it starts increasing on
day 10, reaching values between 6000 to 8000 mg COD/L. This ini-
tial increase can be attributed to the hydrolytic step and has also
been found in other studies (Huilinir et al., 2015; Montalvo et al.,
2016). The increase of soluble COD concentration was more pro-
nounced in the system without ﬂy ash addition and with a ﬂy ash
concentration of 500 mg/L, with soluble COD generation rates of
483.33 and 459.91 mg COD/L d for the system without ﬂy ash and
500 mg/L with ﬂy ash, respectively (Fig. 3d). For the rest of the ﬂy
ash concentrations studied, the generation rate was lower, mainly
because the ﬂy ash addition could stimulate COD consumption
under these conditions. After this initial increase, the soluble COD
starts decreasing due to the action of methanogenic biomass, reach-
ing values of around 3000 mg COD/L by the end of the assays. The
removal percentage for the process without pretreatment was
low, varying between 20 and 43% for all the assays. The soluble
COD removal tendency also differs from that seen in the assays with
pretreatment, showing a clear improvement in the removal when
the added ﬂy ash concentration was greater. This behavior also
agrees with the methane production tendency observed in the pro-
cess without pretreatment, showing that the ﬂy ash for that process
improves the microbial activity and therefore the COD degradation.

Regarding the statistical analysis for soluble COD, it shows that
there are signiﬁcant differences between the system with and
without pretreatment for all the ﬂy ash concentrations studied
(p < 0.05).
Thus, according to these results, it is possible to say that the
combined use of aerobic pretreatment and ﬂy ash as trace element
supplier improved the removal of soluble COD, which was higher
with ﬂy ash concentrations between 10 and 50 mg/L.
It is known that the digested sewage sludge (digestate) can be
recycled by application in agricultural land (Alvarenga et al.,
2015; Brisolara and Qi, 2013); however, it can represent a potential
risk to agricultural soils because of their potential contamination
with heavy metals, organic contaminants and/or pathogens. Due
to the application of ﬂy ash as a source of trace elements that also
contains several heavy metals in the anaerobic digestion, it is
important to know if the digestate complies with current regula-
tions. Chile has Decree-Law No. 4/2009 which indicates the maxi-
mum amount of some heavy metals in order to apply biosolids to
soils. Therefore, the amount of some heavy metals in the digestate
for one of the highest ﬂy ash concentration used (250 mg/L) was
measured. The results are shown in Table 5. It is seen that none
of the heavy metal concentrations in the digestate was higher than
the values recommended by the Chilean regulations for application
to agricultural soils, but the amount of heavy metals in the diges-
tate is higher than the amount found in the ﬂy ash, showing that
the addition of ﬂy ash increased the total amount of heavy metals
compared to the mixed sludge and the ﬂy ash. Therefore, the appli-
cation of ﬂy ash in the anaerobic digestion of mixed sludge does
not affect the feasibility of applying the digestate in agricultural
soils.

4. Conclusions
The combined use of aerobic pretreatment and ﬂy ash improved
methane production when ﬂy ash concentrations were lower than
50 mg/L. Fly ash concentrations higher than 50 mg/L inhibited the
methanogenic process, with lower methane production compared
to the process with pretreatment and without ﬂy ash. VS removal
does not improve by the combined use of an aerobic pretreatment
and ﬂy ash. For the anaerobic treatment of sewage sludge without
pretreatment, ﬂy ash improved methane generation and VS
removal at all the concentrations studied (10–500 mg/L).
